lt1.label: Practice – Question 1
lt1.q: Draw a flowchart with a branching structure for each sentence: a) If someone threatens you online, tell your parents. b) If you get an email with an attached file from an unknown address, do not open the file. c) If a stranger asks you for personal information in a message, do not send it.
lt1.k: All three are if-then structures (one branch). a) “Someone threatens me?” → Yes: “Tell my parents”. b) “Email from an unknown address with a file?” → Yes: “Do not open the file”. c) “A stranger asks for personal information?” → Yes: “Do not send it”. No: continue.

items: a) If it rains tomorrow morning, I will take a raincoat.
b) If I have not finished my homework, I must keep doing it until it is finished.
c) If we have three days off for New Year, my family will travel; if not, we will make another plan.

tin6-chuong-trinh-may-tinh.reading: Read part 1 (textbook pages 71–72). Computers do many jobs quickly and correctly, but we must give them instructions. Computers do not understand instructions in everyday language or in flowcharts. They need a programming language. A program is a set of commands in a programming language. It tells the computer each step of an algorithm. A program takes the input, processes it and gives the output. Scratch is a visual programming language. Other languages are Python, C, Java,… Figure 6.13 is a Scratch program that adds two numbers a and b. Press Run to see the computer do each command.

q1.label: Question – Algorithm and program

q1.k: Input: step 1 ↔ commands ③④⑤⑥ (ask and set a, b). Process: step 2 ↔ command ⑦ (set tong to a + b). Output: step 3 ↔ command ⑧ (say tong). Commands ①② start the program and say hello.
opts: a) Step 1. Input two numbers a and b – commands ③ ④ ⑤ ⑥
b) Step 2. tong = a + b – command ⑦
c) Step 3. Show the value of tong – command ⑧

tin6-thong-tin-trong-may-tinh.tag: Reading Numbers, text, pictures and sound in a computer
tin6-thong-tin-trong-may-tinh.reading:
Read part 1 (textbook pages 12–14).
  • Numbers: in Activity 1, each number from 0 to 7 becomes a string of three symbols 0 and 1. For numbers 0 to 15 we need four symbols. A string of 0s and 1s is a bit string; each symbol is a bit (from Binary digiT).
  • Text: text has characters (letters, digits, punctuation, symbols,…). Each character becomes a bit string by using a code table.
  • Pictures: a digital picture is made of pixels. Draw a grid on the picture; each square is a pixel. In a black and white picture, black is 1 and white is 0. A colour picture needs more bits for each pixel.
  • Sound: sound comes from vibration, for example of a speaker or a guitar string. The speed of the vibration is saved as a number, then as a bit string. Example: a string that vibrates 440 times a second plays the note A: 440 → 110111000.

tin6-tim-kiem-va-thay-the.reading: Read part 1 (textbook page 58). When we type a document, we often need to find a word or replace it with another word. In a short document this is easy. Example: to change “watermelon” to “mango” in an ice cream recipe, use Find and Replace, and every “watermelon” becomes “mango”.
